sec.title: Background
sec.p: This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness and real-world applicability of total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) in patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC), focusing on pathological complete response (pCR) and disease-free survival (DFS) across different chemotherapy regimens.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: In this multicenter retrospective study, patients treated between January 2019 and January 2023, 437 patients with locally advanced rectal cancer who underwent total neoadjuvant therapy followed by surgery were analyzed. Standard fluoropyrimidine-based chemotherapy regimens (CAPOX, FOLFOX, or FOLFIRINOX) were used according to institutional practice, and long-course chemoradiotherapy constituted the predominant radiotherapy approach. Patients were grouped based on chemotherapy sequencing as induction, consolidation, or sandwich regimens. Outcomes were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression for pathological complete response and Kaplan–Meier analysis with Cox proportional-hazards modeling for disease-free survival. The median follow-up duration was 66 months.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The overall pCR rate was 26.3% (n = 115). pCR rates did not differ significantly between induction, sandwich, and consolidation chemotherapy regimens. A longer interval (> 8 weeks) between radiotherapy and surgery was associated with a higher likelihood of achieving pCR. In contrast, cT4 disease and baseline CEA levels > 3 ng/mL were associated with lower pCR rates.The estimated 3-year disease-free survival (DFS) rate was 83.8%. Recurrence rates within 3 years were numerically higher in patients receiving induction and sandwich regimens compared with consolidation chemotherapy, although these differences did not reach statistical significance. In multivariable analysis, poor tumor regression grade, ypT4 stage, ypN + disease, and post-TNT CEA ≥ 3 ng/mL were independently associated with an increased risk of recurrence.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: TNT is effective and feasible in real-world settings, achieving pCR and DFS outcomes comparable to clinical trials. No statistically significant differences were observed in pCR or recurrence rates between induction, consolidation, and sandwich chemotherapy regimens. Prospective phase III trials are needed to compare DFS and OS outcomes across these treatment strategies.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In recent years, total neoadjuvant therapy (TNT) has been increasingly adopted and is recommended by major guidelines as a preferred treatment approach for selected patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC), aiming to improve pathological complete response (pCR) rates and long-term survival outcomes [1]. TNT involves a combination of chemotherapy and radiation therapy before surgery, with the intent to optimize tumor downstaging, facilitate sphincter preservation, and improve disease-free survival (DFS) [2, 3]. However, there remains a lack of consensus regarding the optimal sequencing of chemotherapy, specifically whether induction chemotherapy (before chemoradiation) or consolidation chemotherapy (after chemoradiation) provides superior oncologic outcomes [4, 5]. While the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines recommend either approach, randomized clinical trial data comparing these strategies remain limited, creating challenges in treatment selection [6].

Several landmark trials have evaluated different total neoadjuvant therapy strategies, including induction-based, consolidation-based, and short-course radiotherapy–based TNT, yet results remain heterogeneous[2–5]. The OPRA trial primarily focused on organ preservation, demonstrating higher clinical complete and near-complete response rates with consolidation chemotherapy, rather than being designed to compare long-term survival outcomes [4]. The RAPIDO trial, on the other hand, demonstrated improved treatment outcomes with short-course radiotherapy followed by systemic chemotherapy before surgery, reducing distant metastases [2]. The PRODIGE-23 trial evaluated an intensified, hybrid approach incorporating neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX prior to chemoradiotherapy, showing a significant survival benefit compared to standard chemoradiation [3]. Despite these findings, real-world data assessing the effectiveness, tolerability, and predictive factors of pCR in TNT-treated patients remain scarce, particularly in diverse patient populations.

To address this gap, we conducted a retrospective study evaluating the efficacy and tolerability of TNT in a real-world setting. Our study focuses on comparing induction, consolidation, and sandwich chemotherapy approaches, and on identifying predictors of pathological complete response (pCR) in a real-world multicenter cohort. By investigating these factors in a large cohort, this study seeks to provide clinically relevant insights that may guide future treatment strategies for LARC.

sec.title: Material and methods
sec.p: This retrospective, multicenter study was conducted across 30 centers in Turkey and included patients with LARC who completed TNT before undergoing surgical resection. Patient selection was based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria to ensure homogeneity and adequate follow-up. Patients who initiated TNT after January 2023 were excluded due to insufficient follow-up for meaningful oncologic outcome assessment.
The inclusion criteria were as follows:

list-item.p: Patients who completed TNT between January 2019 and January 2023.

Patients who were planned to receive at least three months of neoadjuvant chemotherapy as part of their TNT regimen (patients who discontinued chemotherapy due to toxicity were included if they received at least two cycles).
Patients who completed the planned radiotherapy component of their TNT protocol.
Patients who were non-metastatic at the time of diagnosis.
Patients who underwent surgery after completing TNT. Patients managed with non-operative management (NOM) were excluded.

sec.p: A total of 610 patients were initially screened across participating centers. Of these, 173 patients were excluded due to metastatic disease at diagnosis, incomplete TNT, non-operative management, or insufficient follow-up. The final study population consisted of 437 patients who completed TNT and underwent surgical resection.

Missing data were handled by case-wise exclusion for the relevant analyses, and no data imputation was performed. Disease-free survival analyses were conducted in all patients with available follow-up data, with follow-up duration calculated from the date of surgery to recurrence or last clinical contact.

Demographic, clinical, and treatment-related data were collected from medical records and institutional databases. The recorded variables included age, gender, ECOG performance status, tumor location, tumor length, T and N stage, extramural vascular invasion (EMVI) status, mesorectal fascia involvement, microsatellite instability (MSI) status, and serum tumor markers (CEA, CA19-9) at diagnosis and after TNT.

Patients were categorized based on the sequence of systemic chemotherapy relative to chemoradiotherapy (CRT). Induction chemotherapy was defined as the administration of at least two cycles of chemotherapy prior to CRT, whereas consolidation chemotherapy was defined as at least two cycles of chemotherapy administered following CRT but before surgery, in alignment with OPRA and CAO/ARO/AIO-12 trial definitions [4, 5]. In addition, in real-life practice, patients who receive (C)RT after induction chemotherapy are given additional chemotherapy until surgery. This treatment approach was classified as a sandwich regimen in our study. In this group, post-(C)RT chemotherapy exposure was heterogeneous and is therefore reported descriptively, including the median number and range of cycles administered prior to surgery. Treatment sequencing was not randomized and reflected real-world clinical decision-making, influenced by tumor characteristics (including clinical stage and MRI-defined risk factors), patient-related considerations, and institutional preference. Surgical planning was performed according to routine clinical practice, and surgeons were not blinded to chemotherapy sequencing.

Treatment-related parameters included the type of chemotherapy regimen (CapeOX, FOLFOX, or FOLFIRINOX), the sequence of chemotherapy (induction or consolidation), the type of radiotherapy (short-course or long-course), completion status of neoadjuvant therapy, and treatment-related toxicities (grade 3–4 adverse events such as neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, diarrhea, hand-foot syndrome, mucositis, hepatotoxicity, neuropathy, and ileus). Treatment-related toxicities were graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE), version 5.0. Missing toxicity data were handled by case-wise exclusion, and no imputation was performed for adverse event analyses.

Standard chemotherapy regimens were administered according to routine clinical practice. CAPOX was delivered using the 3-weekly schedule (capecitabine plus oxaliplatin), while FOLFOX and FOLFIRINOX were administered on a 2-weekly basis. The median number of neoadjuvant chemotherapy cycles was reported descriptively according to treatment sequencing.Radiotherapy was delivered either as long-course chemoradiotherapy (45–50.4 Gy in 25–28 fractions with concurrent fluoropyrimidine-based chemotherapy) or as short-course radiotherapy (25 Gy in 5 fractions), in line with institutional protocols.

Surgical and pathological data included surgical approach (abdominoperineal resection or low anterior resection), margin status (R0, R1, R2), pathological tumor and nodal stage, lymphovascular invasion (LVI), perineural invasion (PNI), and pathological complete response (pCR) status.

The assessment of pathological response was based on the tumor regression grading system. This system, formulated by Ryan et al., categorizes tumor regression as follows: TRG 0 indicates an absence of viable cancer cells, TRG 1 indicates only isolated cells or small clusters; TRG 2 signifies that fibrosis predominates over residual cancer; TRG 3 denotes extensive residual cancer dominating over fibrosis or the complete absence of fibrosis [7]. A tumor regression grade of 0–1 is considered indicative of a good response, whereas grades 2 and 3 are classified as indicating an unfavorable response. Pathological assessment, including tumor regression grading, was performed locally at each participating center according to routine clinical practice, and no centralized pathology review was conducted. Pathological complete response (pCR) is defined by the total absence of viable tumor cells in the post-surgical pathological assessment (ypT0N0); the presence of isolated tumor cells was not considered a pathological complete response.

Follow-up was performed according to routine institutional practice and generally included periodic clinical evaluation and imaging; recurrence was defined as radiologically or histologically confirmed local or distant disease relapse.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Continuous variables were expressed as median (minimum–maximum) and compared using the Mann–Whitney U test. Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages and analyzed using the chi-square or Fisher’s exact test. To identify factors associated with pathological complete response (pCR) and 3-year recurrence, univariate and multivariable logistic regression analyses were performed, with odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) reported. Disease-free survival (DFS) was analyzed using the Kaplan–Meier method, and factors associated with DFS were evaluated using univariate and multivariable Cox proportional-hazards regression models, with hazard ratios (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) reported. In addition to time-to-event analyses using Cox proportional-hazards models, 3-year disease-free survival was also evaluated as a binary outcome (recurrence within 3 years: yes/no) to allow fixed-time point comparisons across treatment groups. In all regression analyses, carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels were dichotomized at 3 ng/mL. This cut-off corresponds to the upper limit of normal reported by routine clinical laboratory assays used at the participating centers and has been commonly applied in prior neoadjuvant rectal cancer studies evaluating pathological response and recurrence [8].
All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA), with a p-value < 0.05 considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total of 610 patients with locally advanced rectal cancer were retrospectively screened across participating centers. After applying predefined exclusion criteria, 437 patients who completed TNT and subsequently underwent curative-intent surgery were included in the final analysis (Fig. 1). Of these participants, 65% were male (n = 286) and 35% were female (n = 151). The median age of participants was 62 years (min–max 28–84). When analyzing tumor location within the rectum, 42% (n = 183) were located in the lower rectum and 49% (n = 215) in the middle rectum. A majority of the patients had clinical T3 (n = 276, 63%) and T4 (n = 100, 23%) tumors, with only 82 patients (19%) showing no clinical lymph node metastasis. Demographic data are presented in Table 1.

sec.title: Neoadjuvant treatment
sec.p: Seventy-six percent of patients (n = 331) received CapeOX chemotherapy, 22% (n = 95) received FOLFOX, and 2% (n = 11) received FOLFIRINOX. Regarding the timing of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, 66% (n = 287) underwent consolidation chemotherapy, while 14% (n = 63) received induction chemotherapy and 20% (n = 87) received sandwich neoadjuvant therapy. The median number of completed neoadjuvant chemotherapy cycles was 4 (min–max 2–12). The majority of patients received long-course radiotherapy (n = 397, 91%).

In terms of completing the planned neoadjuvant chemotherapy, 84% (n = 367) completed the treatment, whereas the remaining 16% (n = 70) did not complete it due to various reasons. The most common reason for discontinuation was hematologic toxicity (5%, n = 20), followed by patient preference (3%, n = 14), neuropathy (2%, n = 8), and other side effects. Grade 3–4 toxicity was reported in 13% of cases (n = 58), with neutropenia (43%, n = 25), thrombocytopenia (26%, n = 15), diarrhea (19%, n = 11), and hand-foot syndrome (16%, n = 9) being the most commonly observed.

Baseline clinicopathological and treatment-related characteristics according to total neoadjuvant therapy sequencing (induction, consolidation, and sandwich regimens) are presented in Table 2. Patients in the induction (85.3%) and sandwich group (83.9%) received more than 12 weeks of chemotherapy during the neoadjuvant period, while in the consolidation group, this rate was 75.1% (p < 0.001). No statistically significant differences were observed between the two groups regarding pathological stages, pCR status, and mRyan regression scores (p > 0.05). The median time between the completion of radiotherapy and surgery was 19 weeks (min–max 5–36 weeks) in the consolidation group, compared to 9 weeks (min–max 2–14 weeks) in the induction group and 13 weeks (min–max 3–19) in the sandwich therapy group (p < 0.001).

sec.title: Pathological evaluation
sec.p: The median interval from completion of total neoadjuvant therapy to surgery was 6 weeks (range, 1–20). Separately, the interval from completion of radiotherapy to surgery was longer, with a median duration of 15.9 (min–max 1–36) weeks, reflecting differences in treatment sequencing, particularly in patients receiving consolidation chemotherapy. Pathological complete response (pCR) was achieved in 26.3% of patients (n = 115), while 73.7% (n = 322) did not achieve pCR. Based on the mRyan TRG scores, a good response was observed in 191 patients (50.5%), while 177 patients (49.5%) did not respond well to neoadjuvant therapy.

Factors predicting pCR were investigated using univariate and multivariate analyses, and are presented in Table 3. A pCR rate of 11.4% (n = 5/44) was observed in the group with a time interval of less than 8 weeks from RT to surgery, compared to 28.0% (n = 110/393) in the group with a longer interval (p = 0.023, OR 3.03 (95% CI 1.17–7.89)). pCR was detected in 18 (28.5%) of 63 patients who received induction chemotherapy, 23 (26.4%) of 87 patients who received sandwich treatment, and 74 (25.8%) of 287 patients who received consolidation chemotherapy. When compared with consolidation chemotherapy, it was found that the pCR rates of the induction group (p = 0.772, 1.11 (0.54–2.29)) and the sandwich group (p = 0.649, 1.15 (0.63–2.11)) were not statistically different. The pCR rate was 24.8% (n = 27/109) in patients with treatment durations of less than 12 weeks, and 26.8% (n = 88/328) in those with longer durations (p = 0.672, OR 0.89 (95% CI 0.54–1.47)). Multivariable analysis revealed that cT4 disease (p = 0.027, OR 1.95 (95% CI 1.09–3.55)), CEA levels above 3 ng/ml at diagnosis (p = 0.072, OR 1.51 (95% CI 0.96–2.40)), and a shorter interval from the completion of RT to surgery (p = 0.035, OR 2.82 (95% CI 1.02–7.41)) were associated with a decreased likelihood of achieving pCR.

sec.title: Disease-free survival (DFS)
sec.p: In the studied cohort, the median follow-up duration and median disease-free survival (mDFS) could not be reached. The Kaplan–Meier curve demonstrating 3-year disease-free survival (DFS) for the overall cohort is presented in Supplementary Fig. 1. Overall survival (OS) outcomes are illustrated in the Kaplan–Meier plot shown in Supplementary Fig. 2. The median follow-up time was determined to be 66.0 months (95% CI: 62.3—69.7). Upon evaluating 3-year DFS, recurrence was observed in 71 patients (16.2%), including local recurrence in 19 patients (4.4%), distant recurrence in 32 patients (7.4%), and both local and distant recurrences in 20 patients (4.6%). Accordingly, the estimated 3-year disease-free survival rate was 83.8%.

Factors affecting 3-year DFS, as evaluated through univariate analysis, are presented in Table 4. Within 3 years, disease recurrence was observed in 12 (19%) of 63 patients receiving induction chemotherapy and in 20 (23%) of 87 patients receiving sandwich regimen, compared to 39 (13.6%) of 287 patients treated with consolidation chemotherapy (induction vs. consolidation: p = 0.269, OR 1.49, 95% CI 0.73–3.05; sandwich vs. consolidation: p = 0.059, OR 1.80, 95% CI 0.97–3.32). Multivariate analysis revealed that having a post-treatment CEA level above 3 ng/ml (p = 0.029, OR 2.09 (95% CI 1.08–4.05)), a pathological stage of ypT4 (p < 0.001, OR 12.39 (95% CI 3.18–48.3)), positive pathological nodal status (p = 0.031, OR 2.09 (95% CI 1.07–4.11)), and a poor pathological response according to the mRyan Regression score (p = 0.003, OR 3.18 (95% CI 1.49–6.77)) were associated with increased rates of 3-year recurrence.

sec.title: Surgical and surgery-related complications
sec.p: Low anterior resection (LAR) was performed in 325 patients (74.4%), and abdominoperineal resection (APR) was conducted in 112 patients (25.6%). One patient (0.2%) experienced postoperative mortality due to sepsis. The most frequently observed complications were surgery-related infections—including anastomotic site abscesses, intra-abdominal abscesses, and perianal infections—wound dehiscence, and wound site infections, affecting 18 patients (4.1%). Details of surgery-related complications are presented in Table 5. No significant difference in the rate of postoperative complications was observed between patients who received induction versus consolidation chemotherapy (p = 0.727). As a supplementary analysis, postoperative complications were classified according to the Clavien–Dindo grading system. Among the 437 patients, a total of 39 postoperative complications were identified. The majority were Grade 1–2 events (n = 25), such as superficial wound infections and minor gastrointestinal symptoms. Grade 3 complications (n = 11) included abscesses, anastomotic leaks, and ileus requiring surgical or radiologic intervention. One patient experienced a Grade 4 complication due to a major vascular injury. The single postoperative death due to sepsis was classified as a Grade 5 event.

The median postoperative hospital stay was 7 days (min–max, 2–62 days). Of the 437 patients, 112 (25.6%) underwent abdominoperineal resection (APR), resulting in mandatory permanent ostomies. Among the remaining 325 patients who underwent low anterior resection (LAR), 274 (62.7%) had protective ostomies constructed during surgery. Of these, 138 patients (50.4%) had their ostomies closed during follow-up, whereas 136 patients (49.6%) remained with permanent ostomies either due to undergoing APR or developing complications that precluded reversal. Consequently, sphincter preservation was not achieved in 136 patients (31.1%). The median time to ostomy closure was 108 days (min–max, 32–242 days).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this multicenter real-world study of patients with locally advanced rectal cancer treated with total neoadjuvant therapy, TNT achieved pathological complete response and disease-free survival outcomes comparable to those reported in clinical trials. No significant differences in pCR or 3-year recurrence were observed between induction, consolidation, and sandwich chemotherapy sequencing strategies. Instead, oncologic outcomes were primarily associated with tumor-related factors, including baseline stage, pathological response, nodal status, and post-treatment CEA levels. These findings suggest that, in routine clinical practice, chemotherapy sequencing within TNT may be individualized without compromising efficacy.

The choice between induction and consolidation chemotherapy (CT) for patients diagnosed with LARC starting TNT remains controversial [1, 9, 10]. While the RAPIDO study preferred consolidation CT, the PRODIGE-23 study opted for induction CT, and both reported similar pCR outcomes [2, 3]. Although the OPRA study found that consolidation chemotherapy could better facilitate organ-preserving approaches, no clear difference was noted between the two methods in patients where organ preservation was not targeted [4]. In our study, patients who underwent induction chemotherapy had higher clinical T stages and other risk factors such as positive EMVI and MRF invasion rates, yet this group received more chemotherapy in the preoperative period. Despite significant differences in clinical staging between the two groups, the similarity in pathological stages could be attributed to the increased chemotherapy received by the induction group. Accordingly, between-group comparisons should be interpreted cautiously, as treatment sequencing reflected real-world clinical decision-making rather than random allocation and was influenced by baseline disease characteristics. Recent real-life cohort studies also found no correlation between pCR and pathological stages with induction or consolidation CT [11]. However, it is important to remember that Phase II OPRA and Phase III CAO/ARO/AIO-12 studies have shown higher CR in patients with similar clinical stages when treated with consolidation chemotherapy compared to induction CT [4, 5]. Our study did not include patients followed with non-operative management (NOM), and choosing consolidation CT might be a more suitable approach for patients planned for NOM. However, for patients without a NOM plan, selecting either approach based on the surgeon's and oncologist's experience appears appropriate.

In our study, the pCR rate was found to be 26.3%, which aligns with the rates observed in other phase III TNT studies reported in the literature [2, 3, 12–14]. While no correlation was detected between the tumor location and pCR, a lower incidence of pCR was noted particularly in patients with cT4 tumors. Consistent with findings from other studies, factors such as cT4, positive EMVI status, and MRF invasion have been shown to decrease the likelihood of achieving pCR. A potential reason for the absence of a relationship between EMVI, MRF invasion, and pCR in our study could be the lack of radiological data available for nearly half of the patients. In conditions like rectal cancer, where treatment plans are heavily reliant on radiological staging, following international guidelines to comprehensively report findings via magnetic resonance imaging is crucial for determining treatment options [15, 16]. Besides cT stage, elevated levels of CEA at diagnosis have also been associated with pCR. Diverse results concerning CEA levels in different patient series have been found in the literature, which is why CEA has not been directly incorporated into treatment algorithms [8, 17]. However, advancements in the field of circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) allow for the dynamic assessment of tumor burden. It has been shown that examining ctDNA before and during TNT is associated with radiological response and pCR [18, 19]. Although our study found an association between CEA levels at diagnosis and pCR, dynamic ctDNA measurements in the near future might provide a clearer determination of tumor burden, possibly influencing decisions regarding NOM or early treatment escalation/de-escalation.

In our research, the 3-year disease-free survival (DFS) rate was determined to be 83.8%.This difference likely reflects real-world population characteristics, as our cohort included a lower proportion of cT4 tumors and MRI-defined high-risk features such as mesorectal fascia involvement and extramural venous invasion compared with pivotal randomized trials. In comparison, the PRODIGE-23 study reported a 3-year DFS rate of 75.7%, and the RAPIDO study reported it as 76% [2, 3]. The relatively higher 3-year DFS rate observed in our study may be attributed to comparatively lower stages of disease among our patients versus those in the other studies. Furthermore, while the PRODIGE study administered 12 weeks of neoadjuvant chemotherapy, three-quarters of our patients received neoadjuvant treatments for longer than 12 weeks. This more intensive neoadjuvant treatment could also have contributed to our results [3]. It was found that ypT4 disease, ypN + disease, and a pathologically poor response increase the rates of recurrence over three years. Literature from other pivotal studies also indicates high recurrence rates in patients who do not respond well to neoadjuvant therapy, particularly those with ypT4 and ypN + disease. Perhaps recurrence rates could be reduced in these patients through maintenance capecitabine therapy or FOLFIRI treatment as seen in the PEGASUS study [20]. With TNT now being a standard practice, there is a need for studies on maintenance/adjuvant chemotherapy post-surgery in patients who do not achieve a good pathological response to TNT. Taken together, disease-free survival in our cohort was primarily determined by pathological disease burden—particularly ypT4 stage, ypN positivity, and poor tumor regression—rather than by chemotherapy sequencing strategies themselves. Elevated post-TNT CEA levels further identified patients at increased risk of recurrence.

Our study, conducted across multiple centers with a large cohort, offers valuable insights into the management of LARC using TNT. One of the key strengths is the extensive patient population, which enhances the generalizability of our findings across various clinical settings. The multicenter approach further supports the broad applicability of our results, reflecting diverse management practices and outcomes. However, several limitations must be acknowledged. The retrospective design may introduce selection biases and limit our ability to establish causality. Moreover, because treatment sequencing was not randomized and MRI-based risk factors were missing in a substantial proportion of patients, residual confounding cannot be fully excluded. In addition, the timing of surgery after radiotherapy was not guided by a predefined or standardized protocol and instead reflected real-world clinical practice across centers, which should be considered when interpreting the observed association between the RT–surgery interval and pathological complete response. Incomplete data, particularly the absence of comprehensive MRI-based staging (including EMVI and mesorectal fascia involvement) for a substantial proportion of patients, reflects the retrospective nature of the study and heterogeneity in MRI reporting across centers and may have limited accurate risk stratification. The relatively small number of patients with mismatch repair deficiency also limited the statistical power of subgroup analyses evaluating its association with pathological response and disease-free survival. In addition, CEA was assessed at predefined clinical time points rather than through serial measurements during TNT, precluding a more detailed analysis of dynamic CEA kinetics. Additionally, variations in surgical expertise and potential differences in the interpretation of staging examinations by radiologists could affect treatment outcomes. These factors underline the necessity for more rigorous prospective studies to confirm our findings and refine treatment approaches for LARC.

Our study confirms the general applicability of TNT in real-world settings, with pCR rates achieved through TNT that are comparable to those reported in pivotal trials. No significant relationship was found between pathological response and DFS when comparing induction and consolidation treatments. Although our findings are promising, they underscore the need for longer follow-up. We plan to provide updated analyses once sufficient follow-up data are available, to offer more refined insights. Specifically, there is a critical need for additional research to evaluate the efficacy of maintenance/adjuvant therapy in patients who respond poorly to TNT. Such studies will be essential for optimizing treatment strategies and improving outcomes for individuals with LARC.
